DLGA-PDE always differentiates through a network; DISCOVER, PySR, PySINDy, LLM4ED and EqGPT's single-case wave mode use finite differences; SGA-PDE offers both and defaults to finite differences. EqGPT's multi-case wave mode and steady mode report none: they take no derivatives from the platform and build their own field representation and evaluation internally.

docs.title: Configurable options
docs.text:
• How SGA-PDE differentiates: kd.Model(algorithm="sga", derivatives="autograd") switches the terminal derivatives to autograd. On a regular, well-resolved grid the default finite differences are computed once and cost you no training run; choose autograd when you want the derivatives to come from a continuous representation of the field.
  • DLGA-PDE's surrogate network: by default the platform trains it from the surrogate settings in kd.DLGAConfig. If you already have a trained field network, pass it through surrogate_model= and that training is skipped.

Every other algorithm has a fixed derivative source, with nothing to choose. For what the data itself must look like, see data requirements.

docs.title: Data requirements
docs.text: KD reads a set of observations and searches for the equation behind them. What it needs from you is two things: a set of coordinate axes, and one or more fields sampled on those coordinates. The derivatives, the candidate terms and the coefficients are all produced by the algorithm.

docs.title: Build a dataset from arrays
docs.text:
kd.PDEDataset.from_arrays wraps arrays you already have. The key order of coords fixes the axis order, and each field array must have exactly the shape given by the axis lengths in that order.

import numpy as np
import kd

x = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 128, endpoint=False)   # periodic axis, endpoint not repeated
t = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 64)
u = np.sin(x)[:, None] * np.exp(-t)[None, :]      # shape (128, 64)

dataset = kd.PDEDataset.from_arrays(
    coords={"x": x, "t": t},
    fields={"u": u},
    lhs="u_t",
    periodic={"x"},
    name="my-data",
)

kd.preview(dataset)

Dataset: my-data
Axes:
     x | n=128  | range [0.000, 6.234] | step 0.04909 (uniform)
     t | n=64   | range [0.000, 1.000] | step 0.01587 (uniform)
Fields:
     u | dtype=float64 | shape=(128, 64) | min=-1.000 max=1.000 mean=0.000 (NaN=0)
LHS: u_t  (field='u', axis='t')
Status: ready to fit

That dataset goes straight into kd.Model.fit(). kd.preview prints, per axis, the point count, range and whether the step is uniform; per field, the dtype, shape, extrema and NaN count; plus the left-hand side it parsed. kd.preview_report returns the same facts as an object you can read from code.

docs.title: Axis and field requirements
docs.text:
• Each axis is a 1-D increasing array: a decreasing coordinate is rejected by from_arrays itself, at construction.
  • Axes are evenly spaced. Finite-difference stencils are written around a fixed step, so an unevenly spaced axis is rejected when the derivatives are taken (algorithms that differentiate a trained surrogate instead are not bound by this).
  • Fields are floating-point arrays with no NaN and no Inf. from_arrays casts coordinates and fields to float64 by default.
  • Axis names are free-form strings, but derivative symbols (u_xx) are parsed against single-letter axis names, so x, y, t save you trouble.
  • periodic marks the axes with periodic boundaries: they are differentiated with a wrap-around stencil, so boundary points keep the interior accuracy. Do not repeat the endpoint on a periodic axis (use [0, L), not [0, L]).

docs.title: The left-hand side
docs.text:
lhs spells out the term on the left of the equation using KD's derivative naming convention; KD parses the field, the axis and the order out of it.

  • lhs="u_t" (default): first-order in time, i.e. u_t = f(u, u_x, u_xx, ...). This is what most algorithms target.
  • lhs="u_tt": second order. The bundled wave and klein-gordon datasets are of this kind. DLGA-PDE is the algorithm that fits them: kd.DLGAConfig(target_lhs_order=2), or the ready-made kd.DLGAConfig.wave_preset() / kd.DLGAConfig.kg_preset(). Every other algorithm builds a first-order evaluator only, and raises at fit() on second-order data rather than quietly fitting a different target.
  • A steady problem has no time derivative and therefore no left-hand side: build it with kd.PDEDataset.from_scatter(..., lhs="") and the equation reads as a sum of terms equal to zero. The three bundled Laplace / Poisson datasets are of this kind.

docs.title: Scattered points
docs.text:
Data that does not sit on a regular grid goes through kd.PDEDataset.from_scatter: every coordinate array and every field array is a 1-D array of length N, one entry per observed point, and the coordinates need not be sorted. kd.PDEDataset.from_xlsx reads the same structure directly out of an xlsx workbook by column header, which fits experimental data already stored as (x, y, u) columns.

Scattered data is handled by EqGPT: its multi-case wave mode and its steady mode declare scattered; every other algorithm asks for grid.

docs.title: Supported layouts per algorithm
docs.text:
Every mode of every algorithm declares the layouts it accepts (topologies: grid / scattered) and the equation forms it searches (forms: EVOLUTION / HOMOGENEOUS) in kd.instrument_schemas(); the spec strip at the top of each algorithm page shows the same information. When the layout or the left-hand-side order of your data does not match the algorithm, fit() raises and names what that algorithm does support.

To try an algorithm before pointing it at your own data, start from the bundled datasets. For how the derivatives are produced, see derivative sources.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
KD is a platform for discovering partial differential equations from data. Seven algorithms live in it as plugins: five published by our group (SGA-PDE, DLGA-PDE, DISCOVER, EqGPT, LLM4ED) and two external baselines (PySR, PySINDy). The platform owns what is not a scientific decision: reading data, computing derivatives, executing terms, fitting coefficients, keeping records, writing checkpoints, drawing figures, running a batch. Each plugin owns its search and the scientific choices inside it.

Data is prepared once and an algorithm is chosen by name:

model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga").fit(data)

The fitted model carries the equation, the score and the record of the run. Changing "sga" to "discover" changes neither that line nor the way the answer is read.

docs.title: Division of responsibility
docs.text:
How to differentiate the data, how to search, how to score a candidate and which equation to hand back belong to the algorithm. What the seven need identically belongs to the platform.

Those services are offered rather than imposed. An algorithm that wants its own scientific path takes it: EqGPT runs two of its modes without platform derivatives at all, SGA-PDE and LLM4ED fit candidates with code they brought with them. What a plugin does not opt out of is the small contract that makes it drivable, and a declaration of what it can accept: which equation forms, which data layouts, where its derivatives come from, what its score is called and which direction is better, which parameters survive a resume. Those declarations are readable at runtime through kd.instrument_schemas(), so a program driving the platform, and the parameter tables on this site, work off the same source instead of a table maintained by hand.

→ Platform and plugins

docs.title: Shared machinery
docs.text:
Derivatives are the clearest case. kd.PDEDataset holds observations only: fields, axes, and which field-axis-order triple is the left-hand side. Derivatives are computed on demand, by finite differences on the grid or by training a surrogate of the field and differentiating that network, following what the algorithm declared it needs. They could not have been stored in the dataset to begin with: the autograd ones come out of a training run that had not happened when the dataset was written.

The rest of the machinery under a search is shared the same way: executing a term string into a column of numbers, assembling the design matrix, solving the least-squares problem, computing MSE, NMSE, R² and AIC, training a surrogate network. Six of the operators route through guarded implementations, so a near-zero denominator or an overflowing exponent produces neither an inf nor a nan. An algorithm that arrives writes its search and inherits the rest.

→ Data requirements · Derivative sources

docs.title: Shared notation
docs.text:
Internally the seven carry different things: SGA-PDE searches expression trees, PySR returns SymPy expressions, PySINDy and DLGA-PDE select columns from a candidate-term library. Before an answer reaches the platform it is written as the same term strings (mul(u, u_x), diff_x(diff2_x(u))), and the equation is assembled from terms, coefficients and a left-hand side. Those private structures never leave their own package: results, checkpoints, figures and batch records all carry the shared notation.

The platform keeps no per-algorithm result format. With one, two equations could only be compared by the string each happens to print, and most of the difference between two such strings is rendering: reorder one KdV candidate library and the same law prints as add(diff_x(diff2_x(u)), mul(u,u_x)) in one run and add(mul(u,u_x), diff_x(diff2_x(u))) in the next. So kd.law_signature reads the set of terms rather than the string, and two equations with the same structure get the same structure_key.

→ Equation representation

docs.title: Score comparability
docs.text:
Each algorithm hands back its own objective value: SGA-PDE reports AIC, lower is better; DISCOVER reports a reward, higher is better. The two are not the same quantity and there is no conversion between them.

The platform does not fold them into one score. Two scores are commensurable when the score_kind, the dataset and the scorer all match, and folding changes none of those three, it only hides that they do not match. To compare, refit the candidate terms against the same data and read the nmse from that fit, which is what kd.evaluate_terms does. That is also why best_score_ stays in the algorithm's own units and is never rewritten by the platform.

→ Score conventions and comparability

docs.title: Figures from one call
docs.text:
kd.VizEngine renders from the per-iteration record inside the result object, so this call does not change with the algorithm:

kd.VizEngine(output_dir="out/kdv").render_all(
    model.result_, algorithm=model.algorithm_, dataset=data
)

Out comes the set every algorithm shares (convergence, parity, residual distribution and field, the equation and the field it reproduces), the diagnostic panels that algorithm declares as its own, and a single-file HTML report. Nowhere does the engine branch on an algorithm's name; which panels are its own is something the algorithm declares. A figure that cannot be drawn is named in the report's warnings instead of quietly going missing, and an overlay of runs whose scores are of different kinds declines to average them and says so on the figure.

→ Visualization

docs.title: Checkpoints and resuming
docs.text:
Point checkpoint_dir at a directory and the run saves its state as it goes, plus a final checkpoint when it ends. kd.load_checkpoint_manifest reads the ledger that directory keeps, so a resume point comes from recorded entries rather than from a glob over filenames.

What a resume restores is the search state; the configuration comes from the new kd.Model. Each parameter carries a tier the algorithm declared: change a resume-safe one and the new value takes effect, change an init-only one and the resume raises, naming the parameter along with its stored and live values. A parameter with no tier registered is treated as init-only, so forgetting to register one costs a refused resume rather than a silent pass.

→ Parameter tiers and resuming

docs.title: Batch studies
docs.text:
One fit answers one question. Research questions are usually plural: does this hold across seeds, across algorithms, across datasets? kd.harness takes an ordered matrix of entries, each an algorithm with a dataset, a seed and its settings, and runs it into a directory that is sealed on write and re-verified whenever it is reopened. An entry that raises is recorded as a failed outcome and the rest of the matrix still runs.

The aggregate then comes from those records rather than from notes. Runs are grouped by the canonical set of terms they selected, and each group reports how far the agreement inside it goes.

→ Batch experiments and evidence

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Batch kd.harness Entry points kd.Modelkd.evaluate_termskd.preview Algorithms SGA-PDEDLGA-PDEDISCOVEREqGPTLLM4EDPySRPySINDy Search the iteration loopthe plugin contractrecordscheckpoints Figures kd.VizEngineplotsreport Core term executionleast squaresmetricsguarded operators Data kd.PDEDatasetderivativesloaders Networks field modeltrainerlanguage-model clients

Each band uses what is below it, and no algorithm's search is built on another's. Figures sit under the algorithms rather than over them because an algorithm declares its own diagnostic panels out of the drawing layer's descriptors, not the other way round.

That order is checked rather than described. An import graph is built on every push and matched against this list, and the list is exhaustive both ways: a new module has to be placed in a band, and a new algorithm has to come out independent of the other six. Neither can be left undeclared without failing the build.

docs.title: The path of one fit
docs.text:
The bands above say what may use what. Read in time instead, a single kd.Model.fit passes through five stages, and the search itself is one of them:

Before The caller builds the dataset. It holds observations and nothing derived from them: fields, axes, and which field-axis-order triple is the left-hand side. kd.PDEDataseta loader, a file, the Hub or a generatoradded noise, if wanted ↓ Setup The fit resolves and checks the left-hand side, reads what the algorithm declared it needs, and assembles that much and no more. An algorithm that declares it needs no derivatives from the platform is given neither those nor an evaluator, and keeps the term executor alone. finite differences, or a surrogate network trained and differentiatedterm executorevaluator ↓ Search One call to prepare, then the same three steps every iteration. This is the whole of the contract: the platform drives the loop and never decides what happens inside a step. propose → evaluate → updatecallbacksone record per iterationa checkpoint per iteration, if a directory was given ↓ Answer The algorithm hands back its final candidate; the platform assembles the equation and the record of the run into one object. The fit returns here. model.best_expr_model.best_score_model.result_ ↓ After Figures and an independent re-check are separate calls, made when they are wanted. Neither is a tail stage of the fit. kd.VizEnginekd.verify_equation

How much of the setup stage an algorithm draws on is its own decision, which is what makes those services offered rather than imposed. DISCOVER uses the shared chain throughout: the platform executes and caches the term columns, solves for the coefficients and computes the metrics. PySINDy, PySR and EqGPT are mixed, with the platform building the design matrix and re-scoring the answer while the algorithm's own backend does the coefficient regression. SGA-PDE runs its own pipeline end to end, down to its own sparse regression, and uses the loop and the records and nothing else.

docs.title: Batch experiments and evidence
docs.text: One fit answers one question. The questions that come up in practice are plural: does this result hold at another seed, on another dataset, under another algorithm? kd.harness runs the plural version and keeps what it ran, so the aggregate can be computed from records instead of from notes.

docs.title: The experiment plan
docs.text:
An ExperimentPlan is an ordered matrix of entries, each naming an algorithm, a dataset, a seed and the settings for that run. Its hash covers the matrix including the order, so the hash identifies the exact study. Datasets are referred to by name and resolved at run time, which keeps the plan itself free of data.

import kd
from kd.harness import ExperimentPlan, PlanEntry, run_plan

dataset = kd.generate_burgers_data(nx=64, nt=32, nu=0.1, seed=0)

plan = ExperimentPlan(
    name="burgers-seed-stability",
    entries=tuple(
        PlanEntry(
            instrument="sga",
            dataset_ref="burgers",
            seed=seed,
            model_kwargs={"generations": 6, "population": 12},
        )
        for seed in (0, 1, 2)
    ),
)
print(plan.name, len(plan.entries), plan.plan_hash()[:10])

result = run_plan(plan, datasets={"burgers": dataset}, store_root="out/burgers-seeds")
for outcome in result.outcomes:
    print(outcome.entry_index, outcome.entry.instrument, outcome.entry.seed, outcome.status)

burgers-seed-stability 3 1ec66c4dac
0 sga 0 completed
1 sga 1 completed
2 sga 2 completed

Widening the study is an edit to those entries: add an algorithm, add a dataset, add seeds. Nothing around the plan changes, and the new matrix gets its own hash.

Entries run one after another. Parallel execution is a separate call that shards a plan across subprocesses, pinning the numerical libraries to one thread per worker, holding the heavy algorithms to one at a time, giving each shard a wall-clock limit and folding the shards back into a single store afterwards, replaying every record and checking that none of them changed on the way.

docs.title: Failed entries
docs.text: An entry that raises is recorded with its error type and message, and the remaining entries still run. Each outcome carries one of three statuses: the fit completed, it raised, or it finished without sealing a record. The one failure that does stop a batch is a failure to write the evidence, on the grounds that a batch that cannot record what it did is not worth continuing.

docs.title: The evidence store
docs.text:
Records are written atomically and never overwritten, and the index is rewritten after every outcome, so an interrupted batch keeps everything that finished. The directory has to be fresh: a store is not appended to.

Reopening one re-checks it rather than trusting it. The plan hash is recomputed from the persisted plan, every record is verified against its own hash and against the plan slot it claims, records under one dataset name have to share one data fingerprint, and a file in the records directory that the index does not list is an error rather than a curiosity. What comes back is read-only. Each store also carries the environment it ran in: the KD, Python and torch versions, the platform string, and the commit when the run happened inside a checkout.

docs.title: Consensus across runs
docs.text:
build_consensus is a pure function over a sealed store. Runs are grouped by the canonical set of terms they selected, so two runs that print differently but chose the same law land in the same class:

from kd.harness import EvidenceStore, build_consensus

store = EvidenceStore.load("out/burgers-seeds")
report = build_consensus(store)
for dataset_consensus in report.datasets:
    for cls in dataset_consensus.classes:
        members = ", ".join(f"{m.instrument}/seed{m.seed}" for m in cls.members)
        print(cls.structure_key[:10], "|", members)
        print("   ", cls.terms)
    for pair in dataset_consensus.adjacency:
        print("adjacency", pair.structure_key_a[:10], pair.structure_key_b[:10],
              pair.relation, round(pair.jaccard, 2))

9f6aa9b928 | sga/seed0, sga/seed1
    ('diff_x(u_x)', 'mul(u,u_x)', 'u_t')
0bb825b5f3 | sga/seed2
    ('diff2_x(sub(u,x))', 'diff_x(n2(u))', 'u_t')
adjacency 9f6aa9b928 0bb825b5f3 overlap 0.2

Two classes out of three runs, and the second one is worth reading before calling the algorithm unstable: diff_x(n2(u)) is the derivative of u², which is 2·u·u_x, and diff2_x(sub(u, x)) is the second derivative of u - x, which is u_xx. Seed 2 found the same law in a different notation, and the adjacency line is where that shows up. Term sets are grouped, not simplified, which is why the report reports a relation between classes instead of quietly merging them.

Each class is described along four independent axes: whether the structure agrees, whether the support agrees, whether the coefficients agree, and whether the empirical fit agrees. They stay separate, and there is no single confidence number folding them together, because the interesting cases are the ones where the axes disagree. Alongside them the report records how far the corroboration reaches, from several algorithms across different derivative sources down to a single run, so a class supported by three seeds of one algorithm is not read as a class supported by three algorithms.

The whole report renders to Markdown and to a JSON artifact, both deterministic: the same evidence renders byte for byte the same way.

docs.title: Equation representation
docs.text:
Everywhere an equation shows up in KD it is the same term strings: an algorithm's input configuration, the answer it hands back, the argument to kd.evaluate_terms. Each algorithm holds candidates in its own data structure internally and converts on the way out.

The notation describes structure, not display. It is not trying to look like the notation in a paper; it is trying to guarantee that one law, whoever derived it, is written as one string.

docs.title: Term syntax
docs.text:
A term is a prefix function call, or a terminal token.

Written Meaning u the field itself u_x, u_xx first and second spatial derivatives, as terminal tokens diff_x(u), diff2_x(u) the same derivatives, as calls diff_x(diff2_x(u)) third derivative mul(u, u_x) u times u_x add(u_xx, mul(u, u_x)) a sum of two terms

The built-in operators are add, sub, mul, div, neg, n2 (square), n3 (cube), recip (reciprocal), sin, cos, exp, log, and lap, the spatial Laplacian: it sums the second derivative over the dataset's spatial axes, so on two spatial axes lap(u) is u_xx + u_yy, and lap(lap(u)) gives the biharmonic term. Six of them route through guarded implementations: div and recip floor a near-zero denominator, log floors a near-zero argument, and exp, n2 and n3 clamp their input magnitude, so none of these six produces an inf or a nan from a zero denominator or an overflowing exponent.

Coefficients are not part of a term: an algorithm hands back terms, coefficients and a left-hand side separately, and the term string describes structure only. Whether two terms are the same is therefore independent of what multiplies them: mul(u, u_x) is mul(u, u_x) whether the fit put -1 or -0.5 in front of it. Writing a constant into a term is accepted (mul(2, u) is a valid term), but the fitted coefficient absorbs it, so it buys nothing.

How far the terminal tokens go is set by max_order (a parameter of kd.evaluate_terms and kd.validate_terms), which defaults to 2, so u_xx can be written directly. Derivatives written as calls are not bounded by max_order, so diff_x(diff2_x(u)) resolves under the default settings (the on-the-fly finite-difference scheme reaches third order).

docs.title: Notation on the input side
docs.text:
Candidate-term libraries and operator sets are written in the same IR as the terms that come back out:

kd.PySINDyConfig().terms          # ('u', 'u_x', 'u_xx', 'mul(u, u_x)')
kd.PySRConfig().terms             # ('u', 'u_x', 'u_xx', 'mul(u, u_x)')
kd.DLGAConfig().library           # ['u', 'u_x', 'u_xx', 'u_xxx']
kd.DiscoverConfig().library.operators
# ['add', 'mul', 'sub', 'div', 'sin', 'cos', 'diff_x', 'diff2_x']

A candidate library assembled for one algorithm can go straight to another algorithm, or to kd.evaluate_terms for a refit. When a library carries a terminal token above the default max_order (u_xxx in the DLGAConfig list above), raise max_order to that order for the refit:

kd.evaluate_terms(dataset, kd.DLGAConfig().library, max_order=3)

docs.title: Conversion per algorithm
docs.text:
• SGA-PDE searches expression trees and maps the node names on the way out: + becomes add, * becomes mul, ^2 becomes n2, and the two derivative operators d and d^2 render as diff_x(...) / diff2_x(...) against the differentiation axis.
  • PySR returns a SymPy expression. It is expanded, split at the top-level sum, and each part is stripped of its numeric coefficient and serialized to IR; the platform refits the coefficients.
  • DISCOVER builds its trees from the IR operator names directly; the operator set above is its own.
  • PySINDy and DLGA-PDE select columns from a candidate library that is already IR.

docs.title: The equation in a result
docs.text:
model.best_expr_ is a display string and each algorithm renders it its own way (SGA-PDE bakes the fitted coefficients into the text), so it is not the thing to align two algorithms on.

The equation-level object is model.result_.equation: terms paired with their coefficients, plus a left-hand side LhsSpec(field='u', axis='t', order=1), that is, u_t.

docs.title: Structural comparison
docs.text:
kd.law_signature(equation) reduces an equation to a signature: the left-hand side joins the term set, terms are sorted in canonical form, and the coefficient vector is normalized with a fixed sign anchor. Two equations with the same structure get the same structure_key, whatever string each of them prints.

Canonical form reorders the arguments of add and mul (they commute) and performs no algebraic simplification, so mul(u, u_x) and mul(u_x, u) are one term. Stopping at commutativity is deliberate: simplification means a body of algebraic rules, and the more rules there are, the less obvious the reason two equations were called the same one.

The two runs below differ only in how the PySINDy candidate library is spelled and ordered:

import kd

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
for terms in [
    ("u_x", "u_xx", "diff_x(diff2_x(u))", "mul(u, u_x)"),
    ("mul(u_x, u)", "diff_x(diff2_x(u))", "u_x", "u_xx"),
]:
    model = kd.Model(
        algorithm="pysindy",
        config=kd.PySINDyConfig(terms=terms, threshold=1e-3, seed=42),
        verbose=False,
    )
    model.fit(dataset)
    signature = kd.law_signature(model.result_.equation)
    print(model.best_expr_)
    print(signature.structure_key, signature.terms)

add(diff_x(diff2_x(u)), mul(u,u_x))
1f62a06976f85133 ('diff_x(diff2_x(u))', 'mul(u,u_x)', 'u_t')
add(mul(u,u_x), diff_x(diff2_x(u)))
1f62a06976f85133 ('diff_x(diff2_x(u))', 'mul(u,u_x)', 'u_t')

The display strings differ, the structure_key does not. That key is what to align results on across algorithms.

Settle on one spelling for the derivatives before you align on it. The canonical form does no algebraic rewriting, so the terminal token u_xx and the call diff2_x(u) are two different terms, and one equation written both ways yields two different structure_key values. Give the algorithms you are comparing libraries in the same spelling: either both u_xxx or both diff_x(diff2_x(u)).

docs.title: Platform and plugins
docs.text: The division that everything else follows: an algorithm keeps its scientific decisions, the platform keeps the work that is identical for all seven. It is what makes seven published methods one library rather than seven scripts sharing a folder.

docs.title: The plugin contract
docs.text:
The contract is small. An algorithm prepares itself against the components it was handed, proposes candidates, evaluates them, updates itself on the results, exposes its best score and best expression, serializes its configuration and its state, and builds its own final result and the target that result is expressed in.

Those members are checked when a run starts, and a missing one raises a single error naming every gap, so an incomplete algorithm fails at the door rather than halfway through a search.

What the platform gives back is the run itself: the iteration loop, batches kept in 1:1 correspondence with what was proposed, callbacks for early stopping and for collecting figure data, checkpoints written atomically from the algorithm's own state, the run record, and the assembled result object.

One thing it deliberately does not do is re-score the winner. The algorithm builds its final result, because the residuals and the target have to come from the same domain, and splitting that across the two sides is how a result ends up describing a quantity nobody computed.

docs.title: Optional services
docs.text:
Derivatives, term execution, the design matrix, the solver, surrogate training: an algorithm uses what suits it and brings the rest. Nothing degrades when it declines, and the ones that decline are not exceptions to the design, they are the reason the boundary sits where it does.

Algorithm What it brings of its own SGA-PDE expression-tree search, its own sparse fit, and its own surrogate when run in autograd mode DLGA-PDE genetic search over a term genome and its own evaluators; the platform trains its surrogate network from the configured values DISCOVER a policy network over token sequences; candidates are scored through the platform evaluator EqGPT a pretrained transformer; two of its three modes run without platform derivatives at all, on evaluators it builds per case LLM4ED a language model proposing candidates, with the finite-difference templates and the sparse fit ported alongside it PySR an external search engine; the platform supplies the design matrix and refits the coefficients PySINDy an external engine whose native coefficients are kept, with the platform refit recorded next to them as a cross-check

docs.title: Declared capabilities
docs.text:
Each algorithm declares what it can accept and what it costs, as data on the class: the equation forms and data layouts of each mode, where that mode's derivatives come from, what its score is called and which direction is better, whether it returns everything in one shot, which parameters exist and which of them survive a resume, and which fields change the scientific identity of a run.

kd.instrument_schemas() returns those declarations, one entry per algorithm:

schema = next(s for s in kd.instrument_schemas() if s["algorithm"] == "pysindy")
print(schema["score_kind"], schema["score_direction"], schema["one_shot"])
print(schema["modes"])
print([(knob["name"], knob["resume_tier"]) for knob in schema["knobs"]])

NMSE min True
[{'name': 'default', 'forms': ['EVOLUTION'], 'topologies': ['grid'], 'provider_kind': 'finite_diff', 'description': ''}]
[('threshold', 'init_only'), ('max_iter', 'init_only'), ('normalize_columns', 'init_only')]

The platform reads the declaration instead of keeping tables of its own: which provider to build, which datasets to accept, how to label a score, what a resume may change. A program driving KD reads the same call, and the specification strips and parameter tables on this site are generated from it, which is why they cannot drift from the code they describe.

The cost class in that entry (light, medium, heavy) is a routing hint declared up front, not a measurement, and it is the one field to read as an estimate rather than a fact.

Algorithms are registered inside the package, and the seven above are what a released version offers; an eighth arrives by being added to KD, together with its declaration.

docs.title: Parameter tiers and resuming
docs.text:
Whether a run can be resumed is decided by which parameter changed, not by the caller.

The parameter table on every algorithm page has a "Resume" column, and every parameter carries a badge there: resume-safe or init-only. The algorithm declares that badge itself, and it is what decides whether a new value takes effect when you resume.

Tier Meaning resume-safe change it, resume from a checkpoint, and the new value takes effect; the stored search state stays valid init-only the new value applies to a fresh fit only; resuming with the change raises

A third tier does not appear in the tables: fields that change the scientific identity of the run (the candidate library, derivative semantics, and the like) are identity-breaking. Changing one makes the two segments a different experiment, and the resume raises as well.

Any config field with no declared tier is treated as init-only. The default falls on the refusing side because of what each mistake costs: a field that should have been resume-safe costs one line of edit, while a resume that succeeded on two different configs leaves the error in the result.

The tables use the config field names. Two fields are spelled differently as kd.Model keywords: num is population, and use_autograd is derivatives.

docs.title: Checkpoint writing
docs.text:
Point checkpoint_dir at a directory and checkpointing starts; checkpoint_every sets the interval in iterations, and a checkpoint_final.pt is written when the run ends. The directory is managed by a manifest.json and refuses reuse: pointing at a non-empty directory raises, so give each run a fresh one. checkpoint_keep_last bounds how many periodic checkpoints are retained; the final one is neither counted nor pruned.

import kd

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
model = kd.Model(
    algorithm="sga", generations=4, seed=42, verbose=False,
    checkpoint_dir="out/kdv-ckpt", checkpoint_every=2,
)
model.fit(dataset)

docs.title: The manifest
docs.text:
kd.load_checkpoint_manifest returns the directory's entries in write order. It is read-only: no repair, no cleanup. Select a checkpoint from these entries rather than globbing the directory yourself.

for entry in kd.load_checkpoint_manifest("out/kdv-ckpt"):
    print(entry.filename, entry.kind, entry.final_status, entry.iteration, entry.best_score)

checkpoint_000000.pt periodic None 0 -18.37657775848694
checkpoint_000002.pt periodic None 2 -18.37657775848694
checkpoint_final.pt final completed 3 -18.37657775848694

An entry also carries best_expression, algorithm, seed, created_at, kd_version and more. kind separates periodic from final checkpoints, and final_status is set on the final one only: completed for a run that finished, crashed for the final checkpoint a crashed run left behind, so the two are distinguishable. Both values have exported constants, kd.KIND_FINAL and kd.FINAL_STATUS_COMPLETED.

docs.title: Resume a run
docs.text:
fit takes a checkpoint path as resume_from. What is restored is search state (the population, controller weights, the current best); the number of generations comes from this kd.Model, and the parameters are judged by the tiers below. seed is not in the tier table, so it falls to the unregistered-field default, init-only: a resume keeps the seed the checkpoint was written with, and a different one is rejected. Changing the seed is a new run, not a resume.

resumed = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=8, seed=42, verbose=False, population=25)
resumed.fit(dataset, resume_from="out/kdv-ckpt/checkpoint_final.pt")
print(resumed.best_expr_)

u_t = -0.0025*diff2_x(diff_x(u)) - 1*mul(u_x, u)

population is resume-safe, so the resume accepts the new value. With the init-only depth instead:

changed = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=8, seed=42, verbose=False, depth=5)
changed.fit(dataset, resume_from="out/kdv-ckpt/checkpoint_final.pt")

ValueError: resume config mismatch for algorithm 'sga': init_only field(s) changed
vs the checkpoint: depth (stored 4 -> live 5). These fields can only be set on a
fresh fit; drop resume_from or revert them.

And with an identity-breaking change, the derivative source (derivatives="autograd", the config field use_autograd):

ValueError: resume config mismatch for algorithm 'sga': identity_breaking field(s)
changed vs the checkpoint: use_autograd (stored False -> live True). A science-identity
change starts a new lineage: run a fresh fit in a new checkpoint directory; this
checkpoint cannot be resumed under the new config.

Every message names the field and both values, so locating the offending change takes no guessing.

docs.title: Add generations
docs.text: generations is not a config field. For the iterative algorithms it maps to the iteration budget, so "run it a bit longer" always works: raise generations on the resuming model. PySR and PySINDy return their full result from a single fit, so for those two generations is not a quantity to raise on a resume.

docs.title: The two manifests
docs.text: The manifest.json above belongs to a checkpoint directory and lists what is in it. A finished run carries a second, unrelated one at model.result_.manifest: the facts needed to reproduce that run, and nothing that varies between two identical runs. It holds the dataset fingerprint, the KD version, the seed, the term library for the algorithms that take one, and, when the run continued an earlier one, where it resumed from.

docs.title: Score conventions and comparability
docs.text:
The platform ranks nothing across algorithms. What it offers instead is one way to refit the candidate terms against the same data.

model.best_score_ is that algorithm's own objective value. Its name and its direction are declared per algorithm: some report AIC, some report NMSE, some report a reward they define themselves, and both min and max directions are in use. The score cell in the spec strip at the top of each algorithm page is exactly these two facts. The same number from two different algorithms is not a comparison.

model.result_.score_kind and score_direction are how to read those two programmatically. score_kind is a stable identifier: two scores are commensurable only when the kind, the dataset and the scorer all match, which across algorithms they generally do not.

docs.title: Refit on one footing
docs.text:
kd.evaluate_terms takes a set of terms back to the same data and fits them once, with the same derivatives and the same least-squares solver. It is one step longer than converting the native scores would be, and what it buys is a number that points at a particular fit rather than at a conversion. Put the term sets you want to compare through that step and the resulting nmse, r2 and coefficients are quantities in one frame.

import kd

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
for terms in [
    ["mul(u, u_x)", "diff2_x(u)"],
    ["mul(u, u_x)", "diff_x(diff2_x(u))"],
]:
    result = kd.evaluate_terms(dataset, terms)
    print(terms)
    print("  nmse", format(result.nmse, ".3e"),
          "coefficients", [round(float(c), 4) for c in result.coefficients])

['mul(u, u_x)', 'diff2_x(u)']
  nmse 8.489e-01 coefficients [-0.0902, -0.0024]
['mul(u, u_x)', 'diff_x(diff2_x(u))']
  nmse 2.903e-05 coefficients [-1.0, -0.0025]

The two sets differ in a second versus a third derivative. The second one is the true support of KdV: the refit returns -1.0 and -0.0025, matching the reference equation, at an nmse more than four orders of magnitude lower. Those two nmse values may be compared with each other, because both fits used the same data, the same derivatives and the same solver.

Besides nmse, mse, r2 and coefficients, the returned EvaluationResult carries condition_number, the condition number of the columns this fit was handed, which is how to tell whether the candidate terms are collinear.

docs.title: The comparison figure
docs.text:
kd.VizEngine.render_comparison overlays several runs: their score curves, a bar chart of final scores and R², and a summary table carrying each run's expression, nmse, r2 and how its term set differs from the first run's.

The mean and standard deviation band over those curves is drawn only across runs that share one algorithm and one declared score kind and direction. Overlay a run reporting AIC with one reporting a reward and the band is dropped, a subtitle on the figure states that the curve trends are not comparable, and the accompanying warning points at the final nmse and r2 instead. Two different algorithms that happen to report the same metric lose the band as well, since one band over two populations describes neither.

docs.title: Accepted term forms
docs.text:
One string is one term, in function-call form (see Equation representation). Infix notation and a top-level sum are rejected with the reason spelled out. kd.validate_terms classifies without fitting, so it can be used as a first pass:

report = kd.validate_terms(dataset, ["u + u_xx", "add(u, u_xx)", "mul(u, u_x)"])
print(report.valid)
for rejection in report.rejected:
    print(rejection.term, "|", rejection.reason)

['mul(u, u_x)']
u + u_xx | syntax: non-canonical term (funcall IR required); Infix operators (e.g., 'a + b') are not allowed. Use function-call IR: add(a, b), mul(a, b), etc.
add(u, u_xx) | composite: top-level additive structure; submit as 2 separate terms: ['u', 'u_xx']

kd.evaluate_terms is strict by default: one rejected term raises InvalidTermsError carrying the complete rejection list, not just the first offender. Pass skip_invalid=True and the rejected terms are dropped, the survivors are fitted, and one warning names what was dropped.

Terminology

model.result_.run_record.evidence.headline_coefficient_source records who performed the fit (native for coefficients the algorithm produced itself, platform_refit for coefficients the platform refitted). It qualifies coefficients, mse, nmse and r2 only, not the score. Score semantics are governed by score_kind.

docs.title: Getting started: discover a PDE from field data
docs.text:
This notebook walks through a compact PDE discovery workflow with kd. We will load a bundled Burgers benchmark with a known equation, inspect the field data, fit a symbolic model in one call, and compare the discovered equation with the ground truth. The final cell keeps the visualization inline so the notebook renders well on GitHub.

import kd

ds = kd.load_burgers()
print(ds.ground_truth)

u_t = -u * u_x + 0.1 * u_xx

docs.title: Look at the data
docs.text:
The dataset contains a field u sampled on an (x, t) grid. Before fitting, kd.preview prints the grid, field, and left-hand-side derivative that kd will use.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

kd.preview(ds)

field = ds.get_field(ds.lhs_field).detach().cpu().numpy()
x = ds.get_coords("x")
t = ds.get_coords("t")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(t, x, field, shading="auto", cmap="viridis")
ax.set_xlabel("t")
ax.set_ylabel("x")
ax.set_title("Burgers field u(x, t)")
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label="u")
plt.show()

Dataset: burgers
Axes:
     x | n=256  | range [-8.000, 7.938] | step 0.0625 (uniform)
     t | n=201  | range [0.000, 10.000] | step 0.05 (uniform)
Fields:
     u | dtype=float64 | shape=(256, 201) | min=-1.000 max=1.000 mean=0.000 (NaN=0)
LHS: u_t  (field='u', axis='t')
Status: ready to fit

docs.title: Fit a model
docs.text:
SGA searches over symbolic expression trees and scores candidate right-hand sides against the target derivative. The generations value is the search budget, so this tutorial uses a small deterministic budget that is still enough to recover a Burgers-like equation.

model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=5, seed=0, verbose=False).fit(ds)
print(model.best_expr_)
print(model.best_score_)

u_t = -1*mul(u_x, u) + 0.1002*diff2_x(u)
-28.776750720652373

docs.title: Compare to ground truth
docs.text:
Read the discovered equation as kd's best symbolic right-hand side for u_t. The exact string can differ from the compact textbook form, but the useful check is whether it captures the nonlinear advection and diffusion terms.

print(f"Discovered  : {model.best_expr_}")
print(f"Ground truth: {ds.ground_truth}")

Discovered  : u_t = -1*mul(u_x, u) + 0.1002*diff2_x(u)
Ground truth: u_t = -u * u_x + 0.1 * u_xx

docs.title: Visualize
docs.text:
kd.viz.plots.plot_convergence draws the best-score curve straight from the fitted result. It reads the recorded score series, masks the non-finite warm-up sentinel so the y axis stays readable, labels that axis with the engine's own score kind (AIC for SGA), and adds a subtitle when the curve is flat (best score reached on the first iteration). The return value is a list of warning strings, empty when the curve was drawn.

from kd.viz.plots import plot_convergence

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
messages = plot_convergence(model.result_, ax)
for message in messages:
    print(message)
plt.show()

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text: The seven algorithms KD supports work in different ways: a population of expression trees, a neural network paired with a genetic search, a policy network emitting expressions symbol by symbol, a pretrained Transformer, rounds of proposals from a large language model, a one-shot sparse regression over a candidate library. Looking at any of them is the same call: hand the fitted result to kd.VizEngine and one call renders the whole set of figures. Switch algorithm= and the figures follow, with nothing new to learn about how to read them. This page is the gallery; Figure generation covers how to render them for your own run.

docs.title: Shared panels
docs.text:
Whichever algorithm ran, VizEngine draws the same group: best score per iteration (the convergence curve), measured against predicted, the equation typeset and as a structure tree, and the residual as a histogram and as a spatial map. Pass the dataset as well and it adds a coefficient bar chart, the field comparison (observed, integrated prediction, difference), the u_t residual field, time slices and an error heatmap.

The three figures below come from one run: SGA-PDE on the KdV dataset that ships with KD, 200 generations, seed 42.

The observations: u(x, t) of the KdV dataset. Every other figure here is computed against it. The discovered equation put back against the data: measured u_t on the left, the equation's u_t in the middle on a shared color scale, their difference on the right. The NMSE of this run is 2.7e-06. The convergence curve: the solid line is the best score per generation, an AIC for this run, where lower is better, settling at −19.42. The dashed line is the same run's population mean, which keeps moving after the best has settled.

docs.title: Each algorithm's own diagnostics
docs.text:
The shared group answers whether the result is right; an algorithm's own panels answer how it got there, so each algorithm declares and draws its own:

  • SGA-PDE, DLGA-PDE: population-level records, per generation the diversity of the candidates, the term count of the candidate equations and the score spread of the survivors, plus the training loss of the neural-network surrogate (filled in only when the platform trained one). SGA-PDE also draws the genome tree of its best individual.
  • DISCOVER: the policy network's training record, per iteration the reward (one curve for the elite subset, one for the full batch), the entropy regularizer and the reward baseline.
  • EqGPT: the reward of the candidate pool per epoch and its spread, plus the cross-entropy loss of each epoch's fine-tune. In multi-case mode it adds the reward of the discovered structure on every case.
  • LLM4ED: the reward spread of the candidate pool per round, the count of invalid candidates, and the cumulative number of language-model calls.
  • PySR: the Pareto front (complexity against loss), KD's independent re-score of that same front, and the two scores against each other.
  • PySINDy: one comparison figure putting the NMSE of PySINDy's native coefficients next to the NMSE of KD's independent refit.
SGA-PDE's three panels, from the KdV run above. Left: distinct candidate expressions per generation. Middle: mean term count of the generation's candidates. Right: mean AIC of the surviving population.

Of the seven algorithms, SGA-PDE is the one whose panels are rendered here so far; the figures for the other six are still to be rendered. The table below lists the panels each algorithm draws from its per-iteration record. Two more are composed at render time and are not in it: SGA-PDE's genome tree, and EqGPT's panels in multi-case and steady mode. At run time plugin.list_plots() returns the complete set.

docs.title: Figure generation
docs.text: Two paths: one call for the whole set, or a single panel drawn onto an Axes you own. Both run after fit, and neither needs any recording set up in advance.

docs.title: One call
docs.text:
import kd

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=200, seed=42).fit(dataset)

viz = kd.VizEngine(output_dir="out/kdv")
report = viz.render_all(model.result_, algorithm=model.algorithm_, dataset=dataset)

print(report.report)
for path in report.figures:
    print(path.name)

Output (out/kdv is created if it does not exist):

out/kdv/report.html
convergence.svg
parity.svg
equation.svg
equation_tree.svg
residual.svg
coefficient_bar.svg
field_comparison.svg
pde_residual_field.svg
time_slices.svg
error_heatmap.svg
plugin_population_diversity.svg
plugin_complexity_evolution.svg
plugin_fitness_spread.svg
plugin_surrogate_training.svg
plugin_genome_tree.svg

Three arguments to render_all decide how far it draws:

  • algorithm= takes the fitted algorithm itself, which draws its own diagnostic panels; those filenames carry the plugin_ prefix. Leave it out and only the universal figures are rendered.
  • dataset= decides whether the data-dependent figures are drawn: the coefficient bar chart, the field comparison, the u_t residual field, the time slices and the error heatmap.
  • animate=True additionally writes a GIF for 2D-spatial-plus-time data, with its path in report.data_files.

Skips and degradations go into report.warnings, so the figure set never shrinks silently. The run above produced exactly one:

plugin plot 'surrogate_training': No data (no surrogate training logged for this run)

That line comes from the algorithm's own plotting code: this run took derivatives by finite difference, trained no surrogate network, and the panel is therefore empty.

report.report points at an HTML report with every figure inlined as SVG, so it travels as a single file; the LaTeX in the equation block is rendered by MathJax loaded from a public CDN. The style= argument of VizEngine takes extra matplotlib rcParams and merges them over KD's defaults. To put several runs side by side, call viz.render_comparison(results, labels=[...]): the convergence curves are overlaid, plus a bar chart of R² across the runs and a summary table.

docs.title: A single panel
docs.text:
To place one panel in a layout of your own, create the Axes and hand it to the algorithm:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plugin = model.algorithm_
print([info.name for info in plugin.list_plots()])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
plugin.render_plot("complexity_evolution", ax)
fig.savefig("complexity.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

data = plugin.get_plot_data("complexity_evolution")
print(data["ylabel"], data["y"][:5])

Output:

['population_diversity', 'complexity_evolution', 'fitness_spread', 'surrogate_training', 'genome_tree']
gen_mean_complexity [1.8235294117647058, 2.34375, 3.242424242424242, 3.026315789473684, 3.6]

The Figure belongs to the caller: render_plot draws only on the Axes it is given, so size, colors and titles stay yours to set. What it returns is the degradation notes for that panel (no data, gaps in the series), and merging those into report.warnings is what render_all does with them.

get_plot_data returns the numbers behind the same panel, ready to serialize to JSON and hand to another plotting library or keep as a record. Its fields depend on the panel; a per-generation curve is {x, y, xlabel, ylabel, title}.

An unknown name raises, listing the names this algorithm has:

Unknown plot name: 'nope'. Available: population_diversity, complexity_evolution, fitness_spread, surrogate_training, genome_tree

For another algorithm, change algorithm= and re-run: list_plots() then returns that algorithm's panels, and both paths above are written the same way.
